name: Streamling
license: Functional Source License 1.1 with Apache 2.0 future licence (FSL-1.1-ALv2): source-available, not OSI open source; each version becomes Apache 2.0 two years after its release
summary: Goldsky’s young Rust pipeline runtime: YAML pipelines of stateless SQL, TypeScript and plugin steps on Arrow, from Kafka or files into Postgres, ClickHouse or webhooks.
intro: Streamling is a single Rust binary that runs one pipeline, described in a YAML file as `sources`, `transforms` and `sinks`. Every stage is an Apache DataFusion execution plan that passes Arrow record batches to the next over in-process streams, so different kinds of step chain freely: DataFusion SQL, JavaScript or TypeScript run per record in a WebAssembly sandbox, calls to an HTTP endpoint, and plugins, which are Rust crates loaded at runtime through a stable ABI. Built-in sources read Kafka (Avro through a schema registry, or JSON), ClickHouse and files on disk, S3 or Google Cloud Storage (Parquet, JSON, CSV or Avro); built-in sinks write to Postgres, ClickHouse, Kafka and webhooks, and track inserts, updates and deletes through a `_gs_op` column taken from Debezium-style `dbz.op` headers. The SQL is deliberately stateless: filters and projections work, joins and aggregations are switched off. For lookups there are dynamic tables, sets of values kept in Postgres that a query can test against and that you can update without restarting. Every few seconds a checkpoint marker flows from the sources through every step; once all sinks have flushed and acknowledged it, the sources commit their Kafka offsets, to Kafka and to a SQLite or Postgres state backend. That gives at-least-once delivery. There is no shuffle between machines: you scale by running more copies in one Kafka consumer group, each checkpointing on its own.

Goldsky, a blockchain data company, wrote Streamling to replace the Apache Flink engine under its pipeline product, and it now runs Goldsky’s Turbo Pipelines. Goldsky published it in June 2026 under the Functional Source License: you may use, change and redistribute it for anything except a commercial product that competes with it, and each version becomes Apache 2.0 on its second anniversary. Goldsky calls it open source, but that licence isn’t an OSI open-source licence. It is new and small: five releases from 0.1.0 (June 2026) to 0.4.0 (September 2026), under a hundred public commits, and fewer than a hundred GitHub stars. The managed way to use it is Turbo Pipelines over Goldsky’s blockchain datasets, at $0.10 per worker hour plus $1 per 100,000 events written after the first million on the Scale plan (checked 2026-10-06).
strengths: Light on resources: Goldsky reports a Kafka-to-ClickHouse workload falling from over 10 CPU cores on Flink to 0.3, and cold starts from over two minutes to under five seconds (its own production numbers)

Extend it without forking: sources, transforms, sinks and SQL functions written as Rust plugins get the same checkpointing as built-in steps, and small transforms can be TypeScript in a WebAssembly sandbox
Arrow from end to end: Avro decodes straight into Arrow batches, and the ClickHouse sink sends Arrow compressed with zstd
Little to restore after a crash: only source offsets live in the state backend, so a supervisor such as Kubernetes can restart it and it resumes from Postgres in seconds
Upserts and deletes flow through to Postgres and ClickHouse, with each batch collapsed to the latest row per primary key
limits: Source-available, not open source: the Functional Source License forbids offering it, or something substantially similar, as a competing commercial product until each version turns Apache 2.0 two years after release
Very young and pre-1.0: public only since June 2026, release notes are empty, 0.3 changed the plugin interface so every plugin had to be recompiled, and most commits come from Goldsky’s own engineers

Not a stateful stream processor: no joins, aggregations or windows in SQL and no distributed state; Goldsky’s answer is to keep state in external databases or use the trigger-based Postgres aggregation sink
At-least-once only: after a restart the gap is replayed, so sinks without a primary key see duplicates
Connector gaps: the Kafka source rejects tombstone records, and the Kafka sink writes only Avro through a schema registry

sections.title: What’s built in
sections.intro: From the README, checked 2026-10-06. Anything else is a plugin.

rows.label: Sources
values: Kafka (Avro or JSON), ClickHouse, files (Parquet, JSON, CSV, Avro; bounded or watched), hybrid (backfill, then a live stream)

rows.label: Transforms
values: Stateless DataFusion SQL, JavaScript or TypeScript in WebAssembly, HTTP handler, dynamic tables

rows.label: Sinks
values: Postgres, Postgres aggregation (trigger-maintained totals), ClickHouse, Kafka (Avro), webhook, print, blackhole

rows.label: State backend
values: In-memory, SQLite or Postgres; holds source offsets, not keyed operator state

rows.label: Delivery
values: At-least-once, through checkpoint markers that sinks acknowledge before sources commit

items.name: Apache Flink
items.text: What Goldsky moved away from. Pick it when you need streaming joins, windows and large keyed state with exactly-once checkpoints across a cluster.

items.name: Arroyo
items.text: Also Rust on Arrow and DataFusion, but with stateful SQL: windows, joins and checkpointed state in object storage. Open source, developed at Cloudflare.

items.name: Redpanda Connect
items.text: The closest match in shape: one Go binary running a YAML pipeline with at-least-once delivery and no state of its own, with a much larger connector list.

story: Goldsky sells blockchain data to developers. Its Mirror product, launched in 2023, let users write a YAML pipeline that kept a copy of on-chain data in their own database, and it ran on Apache Flink: over 3,000 pipelines at once, the biggest on 40 Flink task managers. CTO Jeff Ling says Flink did the job but was hard for anyone outside the streaming team to extend, its checkpoints were hard to inspect, the AWS bill was large, and pipelines took minutes to restart after every change.

A team member’s experiment, a lighter engine to take Kafka data, filter it and post it to webhooks, started in seconds and used a fraction of the resources. Goldsky rewrote the whole platform on it in Rust, on Apache Arrow and DataFusion, kept Mirror’s YAML format, and dropped stateful SQL. The engine became Streamling, and the product built on it, Turbo Pipelines, succeeded Mirror.

On 8 June 2026 Goldsky published the code under the Functional Source License and tagged 0.1.0. Ling credits fast cold starts, a narrow plugin interface and a large saving on cloud costs, and says the team generates many of its plugins with AI coding agents.

choices.choice: No joins or aggregations in SQL
choices.why: Streaming joins need coordination and large intermediate state. Goldsky decided state belongs in external databases with their own high availability, and that a pipeline needing a join has a problem upstream.

choices.choice: Restart fast instead of building for high availability
choices.why: With no keyed state, the only thing to restore is source offsets. If a restart takes seconds, there is no need for standby tasks, hot replicas or state rehydration; a supervisor just starts the binary again.

choices.choice: A runtime with plugins, not a framework
choices.why: Extending Flink meant working inside the framework. A Streamling plugin is a Rust crate implementing one trait, loaded at runtime, so other teams, and code-writing agents, can add steps without touching the engine or crashing other users.
Customers already described thousands of pipelines as sources, transforms and sinks in YAML, so the rewrite could swap the engine underneath without changing what they write.
